criteria.descriptor: Full marks: accurately describes both batch precompute (lookup-time serving, staleness bounded by schedule, scores all users) and online inference (request-time scoring, freshness, latency and feature-retrieval overhead, cost scaling with QPS); correctly states that the session-click feature exists only at request time; and describes feature-store / streaming and training-serving-skew mechanics correctly. Deduct for wrong claims such as 'run batch more often solves it', conflating freshness with the schedule interval, or misstating where latency comes from.

Full marks: covers all requested dimensions — freshness, latency (with the 50ms SLA), cost, feature availability / training-serving skew, and operational complexity — AND commits to a concrete architecture (hybrid candidate-generation + online rerank, feature store, streaming, fallback). Deduct for each dimension omitted or for stopping at a comparison without a design.

Full marks: explicitly reasons that the request-time-only feature is what rules out pure batch, justifies the hybrid split (why keep batch for the expensive/stable part, why do only re-ranking online), and ties the design choices to the stated SLA and cost constraints rather than asserting them. Deduct for unjustified choices or a decision that ignores the given constraints.

Full marks: clearly structured (comparison then design), uses precise vocabulary (candidate generation, re-ranking, online/offline feature store, point-in-time correctness, graceful fallback), and is unambiguous about what runs offline vs at request time. Deduct for disorganized, vague, or jargon-without-meaning answers.

expected_answer_points: Characterizes batch precompute correctly: offline scheduled scoring served via a KV lookup gives very low serving latency but staleness bounded by the schedule, and it scores all users regardless of activity.

Characterizes online inference correctly: scoring at request time on live features is fresh and session-aware and only spends compute on active users, but adds serving-path latency (model + feature retrieval) and requires always-on low-latency infrastructure, with cost scaling with QPS.
Identifies the decisive constraint: the in-session-click feature only exists at request time, so pure nightly batch (even run more often) fundamentally cannot satisfy the requirement.
Proposes a hybrid / two-stage (lambda-style) design: batch for heavy candidate generation or long-term user/item embeddings, plus an online lightweight re-ranker using session features.

Addresses training-serving skew via a feature store with shared feature definitions across offline training and online serving, and point-in-time-correct feature joins, with a streaming pipeline (e.g., Kafka + Flink) populating the online store for session features.
Respects the 50ms P99 SLA: bounded candidate set (e.g., ANN retrieval), lightweight reranker, timeouts, and graceful fallback to the precomputed batch recommendations on failure or timeout.

Discusses cost and operational trade-offs realistically: online cost scales with active traffic vs batch wasting compute on inactive users, plus added monitoring of latency, error rate, feature freshness, and model/feature version parity.
common_pitfalls: Claims batch can be made fresh enough by 'just running it every few minutes' — misses that clicks from seconds ago are still lost and that rescoring 10M mostly-inactive users on a tight cadence is wasteful; the real blocker is that the feature only exists at request time.
Recommends switching entirely to online inference for all 10M users without keeping batch for the expensive candidate-generation step, and without a plan to hold the 50ms P99 SLA.
Budgets only model inference time and forgets the online feature-retrieval latency, and provides no timeout or fallback path when the online layer is slow or down.
Ignores training-serving skew: computes session features online in a way that differs from how the model was trained, or omits the feature store / point-in-time-correct joins entirely.
Treats cost as absolute ('online is always more expensive' or 'batch is always cheaper') instead of noting online cost scales with active QPS while batch pays to score inactive users.
Lists batch-vs-online definitions but never commits to a concrete architecture or a decision for the stated requirement.
reference_answer:
The decisive point is that pure nightly batch cannot meet the requirement: recommendations that react to the last few minutes of clicks depend on a feature — the in-session click sequence — that does not exist until request time. Running the batch job more frequently does not fix this; you would still miss clicks from seconds ago, and rescoring 10M users every few minutes is wasteful because most are inactive.

Trade-offs. Batch precompute is cheap per prediction (an amortized offline Spark job) and serving is a sub-10ms KV lookup, but predictions are stale (bounded by the schedule) and you pay to score every user whether or not they visit. Online inference scores at request time on live features, so it is fresh and session-aware and only spends compute on active users, but it adds serving-path latency (model plus feature retrieval), needs always-on low-latency infrastructure, and cost scales with QPS rather than user count.

Design — hybrid / two-stage. Keep batch for the expensive, stable work: nightly compute candidate sets or long-term user and item embeddings and write them to the online KV store. At request time, retrieve candidates (ANN over item embeddings) and run a lightweight online re-ranker that fuses the long-term signal with session features. Serve the session features (clicks in the last N minutes) from a feature store's online (low-latency) store, populated by a streaming pipeline (Kafka to Flink/Spark Streaming). Use the same feature definitions for offline training with point-in-time-correct joins to avoid training-serving skew.

Operational. Budget the online path against the 50ms P99 SLA (bounded candidate set, small reranker, warm connections); add a timeout with graceful fallback to the precomputed batch recommendations when the online path is slow or fails. Monitor endpoint latency, error rate, and feature freshness, and keep model and feature versions in parity across the offline and online paths. This hybrid keeps the cheap, well-understood batch layer while satisfying the freshness requirement only where it is needed.
